text: Suppose your research plan contains 117 empty response slots. If your pipeline cannot distinguish those slots from real answers, you can create the appearance of data before an experiment has even started. I'm Karishma with Humanitarian's AI. That is why an AI experiment needs an offline dry run. A dry run exercises the structure of the workflow, prompts, run ID, request bodies, recording fields, and validation rules without sending a model request. First, turn the data set into an explicit schedule. Every planned attempt needs a stable prompt, a repetition number, and a unique run ID. The schedule should catch missing prompts and duplicates before collection begins. Next, make planned and observed records

Impossible to confuse. An empty slot should say not run. A real attempt should record what was submitted, when it ran, which model and settings were used, its raw response, and whether it completed or failed. Then test the local workflow. Can it prepare every request without calling the network? Does it preserve the approved wording? Does it stop safely on errors? Does it refuse to overwrite changed files? These checks catch engineering problems before they become research problems. A useful dry run also records the data set version, checksum, configuration, and ordering rule. That creates a traceable contract for what the future experiment intends to do. But a passing dry run proves only

That the plumbing is coherent. It does not prove that authentication will work, that a chosen model supports every setting, that the answers will be high quality, or that the research design is valid. Try it on a small study. Create three prompts, schedule two repetitions each, generate empty slots, and verify that your report says six planned attempts but zero observations. Only then consider a tiny authorized live test. Principle is simple. Validate the experiment before you pay for it, and never let a plan masquerade as evidence. I'm Karishma with Humanitarian's AI.
